cards.title: Distinction between PTA simulations and clinical efficacy evidence
cards.claim: Probability of Target Attainment (PTA) estimates attainment of a specified PK-PD target under a stated regimen and population or scenario distribution; it is not a direct measure of clinical efficacy or microbiological cure. MIC-normalized targets require a specified MIC value or grid for per-MIC PTA; weighting across MIC values additionally requires a relevant MIC frequency distribution. Clinical exposure-response evidence can inform efficacy but does not alone establish causal clinical efficacy, and such analyses may be infeasible or confounded.
conditions: Applicable when evaluating the evidentiary weight of simulated exposure metrics.
Relevant when distinguishing between nonclinical PK-PD targets and clinical outcomes.
Applies to antimicrobial agents where PTA is used to justify dose selection prior to pivotal efficacy trials.
required_inputs: Nonclinical PK-PD targets (PDTs) derived from in vitro/in vivo models.
Population PK models (initially from healthy volunteers, later from patients).
Clinical E-R data (if available) to validate or refine nonclinical targets.
limitations: PTA does not account for host factors, adherence, or complex disease states unless explicitly modeled.
Clinical E-R analyses may be impossible if patient numbers are low, success rates are high (lack of failures), or outcomes are confounded by combination therapy.
Simulations cannot replace clinical data for establishing safety or efficacy claims; they only support the rationale for dose selection.
cards.downstream_use: Use PTA to justify dose selection in regulatory submissions, but explicitly state that it is a predictive tool, not proof of clinical cure. Do not interpret high PTA as guaranteed clinical success.
cards.retrieval_keywords: Why prospective exposure or target attainment cannot establish human efficacy or safety

note: Method/reference scope retained; source identity is available in original evidence.
